1: Says the name is literally Judas and that the best evidence makes him the half-brother of Jesus named in Matthew 13:55; that he called himself only a bondservant of Jesus Christ shows his humility.
Jude the apostle, whom Matthew and Mark call Thaddeus in the Gospel, writes against the same corruptors of the faith whom both Peter and John condemn in their Epistles.
2: Daily Study Bible · What It Means to Be a Christian · vv.1–2

Barclay says Jude was content with second place, known only as the brother of the more famous James, and that the one title he claimed was servant of Jesus Christ; Christians, he says, are people called by God, loved by God and kept by Christ.

Indeed mercy, for we have been recalled and taken by Him into ministry because of the bowels of the mercy of God: peace, however, because God the Father Himself has granted this to us, bringing us who had sinned back to His friendship through His Son Jesus Christ: and love, indeed, because of the love He had for us, His only-begotten Son was exposed to death for us.
3: Daily Study Bible · Defending the Faith · v.3

Barclay says Jude set aside a treatise on the faith to write a tract for the times; the faith is something handed down, not invented, and each generation must hand it on unspoiled, a defense that may be costly, as the Greek word behind “agony” suggests.

Says this was the letter that did not want to be written; the word for “contend” comes from the wrestling mat, and “the faith” means the essential truths of the gospel that all true Christians hold in common.
The call to defend the faith
Exhorting them not to learn another faith than that which was once delivered to them by the apostles, but always to contend for it even unto death.
4: Daily Study Bible · The Peril from Within · v.4

Barclay says the danger came from inside the church: the Greek word pictures men slipping in by stealth, and he takes them to be teachers who twisted grace into an excuse for open immorality and who thought too little of Jesus Christ.

But they pervert this grace of His into licentiousness, who now sin all the more freely and easily, as they see themselves less immediately examined by the harshness of the law for their admitted crimes.
5: Says Jude recalls Numbers 14 and Kadesh Barnea: a people who had seen God’s rescue at the Red Sea still fell into unbelief, started well and did not endure to the end.
The example of the people of Israel
For just as he first saved the humble who cried out to him from the affliction of Egypt, he later cast down the proud who murmured against him in the wilderness.
6: Says Jude is known for raising obscure points and links this one with Genesis 6; by not keeping their place these angels are now kept in chains, and their pursuit of freedom put them in bondage.
The example of the angels who sinned
And in this sentence, as in the previous one, we must first remember that Jesus our Lord punished the transgressing angels.
7: Daily Study Bible · The Dreadful Examples · vv.5–7

Barclay says Jude reminds his readers of three things they already know (Israel in the wilderness, the fallen angels and Sodom) to show that privilege is no protection and that sin and judgment go together, so that the offenders may repent in time.
Says Sodom and Gomorrah were prosperous, privileged places, as Ezekiel 16:49 shows, and that their past blessings did not keep them from judgment.
The example of Sodom and Gomorrah

Because He had given an example of condemnation in those who solely deny the Sovereign and our Lord Jesus Christ, by recalling the ruin of the murmuring and unfaithful people in the desert, or those rising against the author of the wicked angels, so He gives an example of the punishment of those who turn the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into licentiousness, recalling the burning of Sodom.
8: “How to Identify Terrorists in the Church”
Daily Study Bible · Contempt for the Angels · vv.8–9

Barclay compares these men to the false dreamers of Deuteronomy 13 and says their teaching led them to defile the flesh and to despise angels; if Michael would not speak evil even of the devil, no human being may speak evil of an angel.

It must be understood that these, like the Sodomites who defiled the flesh, are also to be damned, like the unbelieving people who blasphemed the majesty of divine power, like the angels who despised the dominion of their Creator.
9: Daily Study Bible · Contempt for the Angels · vv.8–9

Barclay compares these men to the false dreamers of Deuteronomy 13 and says their teaching led them to defile the flesh and to despise angels; if Michael would not speak evil even of the devil, no human being may speak evil of an angel.

Says Michael is named in Daniel 10 and 12, Revelation 12 and here, always in a setting of battle, and that his way of fighting is a model: he did not rely on his own authority but said, “The Lord rebuke you!”
From which Scriptures Jude took this testimony is not easily clear. But it should be known that we find something similar to these things in the prophet Zechariah.
10: Daily Study Bible · The Gospel of the Flesh · v.10

Barclay says these men sneer at whatever lies outside their experience and are ruled by the instincts they share with animals; a person who goes on refusing to listen to God ends up unable to hear him at all.
Says that unlike Michael these men spoke evil of people and things they did not even know, and that for all their claims to be spiritual their only knowledge was natural.
But the archangel did not dare to bring a railing accusation against the Devil, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” How do these men dare to blaspheme the glorious beings?
11: Daily Study Bible · Lessons from History · v.11

Barclay says that in Jewish tradition Cain stood for the cynic who denies judgment as well as the murderer, Balaam for greed and for teaching others to sin, and Korah for the man who will not accept authority and grasps at what is not his.

Says the way of Cain is unbelief and empty religion that ends in jealousy and anger, the error of Balaam is a willingness to compromise anything for money, and the rebellion of Korah is the rejection of the leaders God appointed.

They go in the way of Cain, who assume for themselves the name of learned men out of envy for their betters to be honored. And they pour themselves out in the error of Balaam, who for the love of earthly goods, attack the truth which they themselves know.
12: Daily Study Bible · The Picture of Wicked Men · vv.12–16

Barclay prefers “hidden rocks” to “blots” for Jude’s rare word and says these men were using the Love Feasts as cover for their lusts, like sunken rocks on which the fellowship of the church could be wrecked.

But heretics are clouds without water, who have placed their mouth in the heavens by their proud words; but they do not water the hearts of their listeners with the water of wisdom, who are carried away by the winds, as if by the suggestion of invisible spirits, and are caught up in various errors of vices.
13: Compares the love feasts to a potluck dinner at which these men served only themselves, and takes the pictures in turn: clouds that give no rain, trees with no fruit when fruit is due, a restless sea, and stars no one can steer by.

The wild waves of the sea are perverse teachers, who are always restless in themselves, swollen, dark, and bitter, and never cease to attack the peace of the Church, which is the stability and firmness of the faithful.
14: Says the Book of Enoch was not received as Scripture but was respected by Jews and early Christians, and that Jude stresses two words in the quotation: “all” and “ungodly.”
He does not speak against all men, but against all the impious, leaving none of them unpunished.
15: Daily Study Bible · The Fate of Disobedience · vv.12–16

Barclay pictures the litter that storm waves leave on the shore, bleached like bones on the Dead Sea, and says that Jude, a devout Jew who knew and loved the Book of Enoch, quotes it naturally because his readers knew and respected it.
Says the Book of Enoch was not received as Scripture but was respected by Jews and early Christians, and that Jude stresses two words in the quotation: “all” and “ungodly.”

This sentiment is indeed true, because the Lord, coming in judgment, will convict the impious not only of deeds but also of words, and will judge the wicked; however, it should be known that the book of Enoch, from which this is taken, is classified among the apocryphal Scriptures by the Church, not because the sayings of such a great patriarch can be in any way dismissed or should be considered false, but because the book offered under his name does not seem to have been truly written by him, but published by another person under his title.
16: Daily Study Bible · The Characteristics of Evil Men · vv.12–16

Barclay says Jude uses one word familiar to Jews, the murmuring of Israel in the desert, and one familiar to Greeks, the man who always blames his lot; such people boast before those they want to impress and flatter those they think important.
The more anyone murmurs and grumbles about the present labors of the Church, the less they have extinguished the desires of the flesh within themselves.
17: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 1
Daily Study Bible · The Characteristics of Error (1) · vv.17–19

Barclay says nothing had happened that the apostles had not foretold; the words Jude quotes are in no New Testament book and may come from a lost writing, from preaching he had heard, or from the sense of a passage such as 1 Timothy 4, and those who mock the moral law do so because they want their own way.

“remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles,” those by Peter in the second Epistle, and by Paul in almost every epistle. From this, it is clear that this was written last after the apostles had passed away.
18: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 1
Daily Study Bible · The Characteristics of Error (1) · vv.17–19

Barclay says nothing had happened that the apostles had not foretold; the words Jude quotes are in no New Testament book and may come from a lost writing, from preaching he had heard, or from the sense of a passage such as 1 Timothy 4, and those who mock the moral law do so because they want their own way.
Says their methods all had to do with words, complaining, boasting and flattery, and that the answer to such dangers is to remember the words of the apostles.

For they are not the only ones, Jude says, who perish, but they also rob the nourishments of those of the Church, (for this is what the term “cause division” intends to signify), that is, making them outside the ecclesiastical boundaries, either of the faith or even of the very holy tabernacle of the Church.
19: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 1
The Holy Spirit and the One Church
Says these men were not spiritual at all but ruled by natural instincts, with a bent toward separating themselves and causing divisions.

Therefore, they reprobate themselves by separating from the lot of the righteous, hence they are sensual, that is, following the lusts of their own soul, because they have not merited to possess the Spirit of unity by which the Church is gathered together, by which it is made spiritual.
20: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 2
We pray in the Holy Spirit when, pierced by divine inspiration, we seek heavenly aid to receive the goods which we cannot possess by ourselves.
21: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 2
“keep yourselves in the love of God,” that is, safeguard yourselves, waiting for the mercy of our Lord that leads to eternal life.
22: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 2
Daily Study Bible · Reclaiming the Lost · vv.22–23

Barclay notes that the Greek text here is uncertain and says that even with the worst offenders the Christian’s duty is to save and not to destroy; some are to be argued out of error, some snatched from the fire, and some helped only by those who are very sure of their own faith.
Says those who have been influenced are to be treated according to where they are: some with compassion, and others confronted more strongly, but in fear and never with a sense of superiority.

What he said with fear must be joined to all three things he proposed. Because whoever reproves apostates and shows them as damnable must act in fear, lest perhaps he or his loved ones suffer something similar.
23: Learning to Pray in the Spirit and the Word, Part 2

By “garment of the flesh” he means our body. However, we should not hate our body, but we should hate this stained condition in every way, and as much as we can act to make it spotless, so that what is carnal may deserve to become spiritual.
24: Glory, Majesty, Dominion, and Authority Keep Us Safe for Everlasting Joy
Christians Kept in Time and Glorified in Eternity
Daily Study Bible · The Final Ascription of Praise · vv.24–25

Barclay says the New Testament three times praises the God who is able (Romans 16, Ephesians 3 and here); the word for “from stumbling” was used of a sure-footed horse, and the letter ends with the certainty that behind everything stands a God whose name is Savior.

It rightly says here that we will be placed in exultation before the presence of God's glory, whom he previously admonished to serve God in fear. For the more fearful we are about our actions in the present, the more we will rejoice about our deserved reward in the future.
25: Glory, Majesty, Dominion, and Authority Keep Us Safe for Everlasting Joy
Christians Kept in Time and Glorified in Eternity

Says that after so much warning the readers might have been discouraged, and the doxology reminds them of God’s care and their destiny: they will not slink into God’s presence but be presented there with great joy.
This clause attributes equal and co-eternal glory and kingdom to both the Father and the Son, before all and through all ages.
